articles.title: Xbox CEO is reportedly planning three more rounds of job cuts; starting this month, layoffs are part of what CEO Asha Sharma described as 'fundamental reset of how Xbox operates and invests'
articles.summary: Microsoft’s Xbox division is reportedly preparing for three additional rounds of layoffs over the coming months as CEO Asha Sharma pushed ahead with a
articles.body: Microsoft’s Xbox division is reportedly preparing for three additional rounds of layoffs over the coming months as CEO Asha Sharma pushed ahead with a sweeping restructuring aimed at improving the gaming business’ financial performance. According to a report by Fortune, Sharma is planning some more job cuts this month, followed by some additional rounds in November and January, extending a shake-up that has already resulted in thousands of layoffs across Microsoft’s gaming operations. In July this year, Asha Sharman announced plans to eliminate approximately 3,200 jobs during Microsoft's fiscal 2027, including around 1,600 positions that were cut immediately. A further round of layoffs affecting roughly 260 employees followed in September. Microsoft has not publicly confirmed the latest reported plans or disclosed how many employees could be affected.'Fundamental reset' of Xbox operationsThe layoffs are part of what Asha Sharma has previously described as a fundamental reset of how Xbox operates and invests. In a message to employees earlier this year, she said the business was not healthy and acknowledged that Xbox was operating with margins significantly below those of comparable platform and publishing companies.Sharma argued that years of heavy investment in content, hardware, platforms and studio acquisitions had failed to deliver the level of growth Microsoft expected. The restructuring is aimed at simplifying the organisation, reducing costs and focusing resources on projects with stronger commercial prospects.Xbox job cuts: Employees demoralisedSpreading the cuts over several waves has left some employees demoralised, Fortune reports. Some staff feel they are working under a yearlong cloud, waiting to see whether their roles will be next. Fortune also found at least one employee who was laid off and then offered a chance to stay. Some employees appreciated Sharma’s transparency, the report says. Sharma acknowledged the tough decisions but said she values people and does not intend to be transactional.Studios and strategy under reviewThe reset has already resulted in major changes across Microsoft's gaming portfolio. Studios including Double Fine Productions and Compulsion Games have been allowed to regain independence, while other teams have undergone reviews, reorganisations or ownership discussions as Xbox streamlines its operations.The restructuring reflects growing pressure on Microsoft's gaming division to improve profitability amid rising industry costs and a challenging console market. While speculation has emerged over Xbox's long-term future within Microsoft, Sharma recently told media outlets that Xbox is not for sale, while Microsoft executives have publicly backed her leadership of the gaming business.Why Xbox is being resetSharma, 38, took over in February from longtime Xbox head Phil Spencer. She had no video game industry experience, having previously led product work on Microsoft’s AI Foundry platform. Fortune describes Xbox as a roughly $21 billion business with profit margins of about 3 percent, a fraction of what rivals earn and far below what Microsoft expects of its major units. Current Xbox consoles have sold only a little over a third as many units as the PlayStation 5, according to third-party estimates, and memory chip shortages are pushing up hardware costs. Sharma told Fortune in July that Xbox had grown by making many bets and lost focus on its core business, saying the company “spread ourselves too thin.”Questions about Xbox’s futureSeveral current and former staff members told Fortune they believe Xbox is being prepared for a possible sale, spinoff or other restructuring, amid heavy Microsoft spending on artificial intelligence. Judson Althoff, one of Microsoft’s most senior executives, rejected that idea, saying Microsoft would not have put Sharma in charge of a business it intends to sell. The next test comes with Microsoft’s quarterly earnings report this month, and Sharma has said she expects financial improvements to show in Microsoft’s fiscal 2027.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fans React to Shrek 2 Remastered's Surprising PC Requirements
articles.summary: Shrek 2 isn’t exactly pushing the bounds of PC graphics, but the recommended specs for the remaster are surprisingly hefty.
articles.body:
Shrek 2 isn’t exactly pushing the bounds of PC graphics, but the recommended specs for the remaster are surprisingly hefty. Originally released in 2004, this remaster boasts better textures, enhanced UI, 4K resolution — and, it seems, a beefy PC.

According to the Steam page , to even run Shrek 2 Remastered you’ll need a GeForce RTX 4060 or RTX 3060 Ti graphics card or equivalent. The developer recommends a GeForce RTX 4070 or RTX 5070 to get the best experience. What have they been feeding him? Have a look at the screenshots in the slideshow, below, to get a sense of what to expect.

“Those swamp graphics better be baller,” said one X / Twitter user . Another complained that they’re able to run Red Dead Redemption 2 at the highest settings, but their PC would apparently struggle with this makeover of a 22-year-old game.

“Seems a bit much for a remaster of a GameCube game but if that’s what we need to render Shrek’s highly detailed green skin then so be it,” said another Twitter user . “They went full in with the GTA 6 aesthetics,” said another .

Other posts expressed concern over it being a “vibe coded” remaster, but there’s currently no AI disclosure on Steam to suggest that’s the case. Valve asked developers to specify when they use AI during game creation or marketing.

Shrek 2 Remastered was revealed alongside a trailer that parodied GTA 6 , and is set to launch just over a week before Rockstar’s behemoth, on November 10. Despite the parody trailer, no one expected it to have similar graphical demands as GTA 6, but here we are. You’ll need 12-16GB of VRAM for this beast. It’s a bit ogre the top.

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: Resident Evil Requiem made more money from PS5 discs than from all copies on Xbox.
articles.summary:
That’s according to analyst Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics, in a wider report on revenue from physical PlayStation games ahead of their elimination. 30 percent of Requiem’s PS5 revenue came from disc sales, exemplifying two trends Elliott finds: single-player AAA titles are especially reliant on discs, and the Japanese market is uniquely disc-centric.

articles.title: Crimson Desert Charting the Unknown DLC Features Revealed, Including Shipbuilding, Romance, and Housing
articles.summary: Pearl Abyss has pulled back the curtain on the upcoming Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, revealing what players can expect. Here's a rundown of all the new features, systems, and mechanics.
articles.body:
Pearl Abyss has pulled back the curtain on the upcoming Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, revealing what players can expect.

Charting the Unknown adds new stories, ocean exploration, romance, business management and expanded housing to an already feature-packed Pywel. We have everything you need to know about the major additions below.

There are character focused stories for playable characters Kliff, Damiane, and Oongka, who, having put the fight for the Greymanes and Pywell to bed, set out on new paths. They’ll encounter allies and threats “both old and new.” Based on the new overview video, these new individual character stories will be relatively involved, with cutscenes pushing the plot forward.

The DLC expands the Great Ocean of Pywel area, which you might have crossed in the base game on the back of a dragon. After establishing the Greymane camp, you can unlock shipbuilding, then gather resources to build your own vessel and customize it before you set sail. Pearl Abyss said that you’ll fight enemies (there’s ship combat), establish new strongholds with the Greymanes, and earn new rewards.

You can craft your own dive suit to help you delve deeper into the ocean. “More secrets lie beneath the surface, where new underwater traversal methods let players dive below the waves to uncover sunken ruins, treasure and resources,” Pearl Abyss said, while showing off the ability to hitch a ride on the back of a sea creature.

If you earn the trust of certain characters you can develop romantic relationships and even marry, Pearl Abyss said. One potential romance option is Bari, the Witch of Kindness. Pictures shown reveal a number of dialogue options tied to this mechanic, including "Give a genuine compliment," and "Confess your feelings." “Close” companions may also visit the Greymane Camp to “spend some time together.”

As for housing, you will be able to design the structure of your home from the ground up, including the placement of walls, windows and other structural elements. This sounds fun: once you’ve liberated certain castles, you can claim them and decorate their interiors, turning it into a new home.

In the base game, once the Greymane camp was established, you could send comrades on missions to liberated strongholds. With the DLC, you can manage some of these locations directly. You can now lease facilities across Pywel, assign comrades and equipment, choose which goods to sell, and decide how best to run each business to grow its recognition and profits.

Pearl Abyss said “seasoned fighters seeking a greater test” should consider the new challenge where players face a series of powerful bosses from across Pywel, one after another. If you do well, expect "valuable rewards."

As someone put Crimson Desert down some time ago having sunk over 100 hours into the game, I'm feeling the pull to return to the game for the DLC. Pearl Abyss' relentless pace of updates in the wake of Crimson Desert's launch earlier this year made significant improvements and added game-changing features, but the new systems and mechanics coming with Charting the Unknown clearly take things to a new level. Even if you're not into story side of things, there's plenty to fuss over. The business management system, for example, looks like tens of hours of gameplay alone. Then there's underwater exploration and what I'm sure will end up a fan-favorite: romance.

Crimson Desert Enhanced: Charting the Unknown launches on October 29, 2026 at 2pm PT, 5pm ET, 10pm UK time, on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store.

articles.title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 – Detailed Impressions of the Necron and AdMech Factions | IGN Preview
articles.summary: I had a great time getting chromed up with the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Necrons in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4. The campaign story really starts to come together in some interesting ways in its second chapter. And the ways both of these factions control space differently feel like engaging and welcome additions to the roster compared to the more straightforward playstyle of Orks and Space Marines.
articles.body:
The Adeptus Mechanicus and Necron factions play significantly differently from the previous two we looked at.

The AdMech campaign story features some alluring intrigue.

A few weeks ahead of release, there are still a few technical rough spots.

The Terminator-like Necrons and the cybernetic humans of the Adeptus Mechanicus make a very interesting match-up on the battlefields of Warhammer 40K. At first glance, you might ask yourself why Dawn of War 4 spent two of its faction slots on what could broadly be described as "robot guys." And certainly, they do have some similarities. But now that I've gotten to spend quite a bit of time with both, I can say that they certainly claim their own niches.

While the demo I got to check out also included Space Marines and Orks, those missions were the exact same ones we covered extensively as part of our exclusive IGN First coverage earlier this year. Of course, they've gotten a lot of polish since then. But in terms of the campaign especially, it's a lot of stuff we've already covered. So go check those videos out if you haven't. Because here, I'm going to focus on the stuff that was brand new to me: the AdMech and the Necrons.

We got to see the first six missions of the AdMech campaign, and the tone is quite a bit different from the Orks. While we last left warbosses Guzcutta and Goregutz scrapping over who got to be da biggest boss, not really caring about who got in their way or why, playing as AdMech let me engage with the unfolding events on Kronus much more proactively.

It's the second campaign of the four if you want to go in chronological order, and your choices in the Ork campaign can carry over in certain ways. Whether you chose to elevate the beastboss or the warlord from the stars to power might affect what kinds of Ork enemies you face, for instance. But the Orks play more of a supporting role than anything in these six missions, as the followers of the Omnissiah are focused on the much deeper problem of the Necron presence on Kronus.

Our main hero for the AdMech is Potentia-Delta-9, a technoarchaeologist who often puts the quest for knowledge above the directives of her superiors. She eventually locks dendrites with Sek-Ix-23, a much more by-the-book machine cultist who doesn't appreciate her loose cannon way of doing things. Just like the Ork campaign eventually split off to let you play as Guzcutta or Goregutz, the AdMech story reaches a point where the Magos Dominate of Kronus – the highest-ranking commander of the Mechanicus forces – gives a final ultimatum to Potentia. You can continue playing as her and go rogue, or choose to take over as Sek-Ix and try to restore order.

The story structure is a bit different from the Ork campaign in that it's not actually a branching timeline here. The same story will play out either way, but Potentia's perspective on it is quite different from that of Sek-Ix. They eventually come together before the end, but I don't want to spoil exactly how. I enjoyed this campaign a fair bit more than the Ork one overall. The stakes are higher, the characters are more relatable, and there's some juicy intrigue and ancient secrets to dig into.

The AdMech faction plays very differently from the Orks, as well. They're highly ranged-focused, with basic Skitarii Rangers and Skitarii Vanguards as the backbone of their armies. Both prefer not to get into melee if they can help it. But Vanguards are a bit more durable and excel at medium range, while Rangers file in behind them to lay down fire from a distance. They also get access to Ruststalkers, deadly melee troops who are permanently cloaked until they enter combat or get very close to the enemy.

While these cybernetic humans do a lot of the dirty work, the AdMech specialists come from the higher tech Cult of the Omnissiah. Tracked Kataphron melt through armor with great ease and elite Kastelan Robot maniples transform the frontline into a chrome wall of death in the late game. They're an adaptable army that can get shredded in close quarters if you're not careful, but has tools for almost any situation.

Their buildings form a network called the Noosphere that grows in power the more structures are connected to it, granting bonuses to all structures in the network. This can increase the power of defensive turrets or the production speed of unit structures, for example. But you need either cheap, defenseless Cogitator Relays or more expensive Cognis turrets to link distant structures and resource points to the network, and anything that gets cut off from your main base loses all of the benefits of the Noosphere.

This makes the AdMech somewhat vulnerable to flanking and deep-strike tactics, and creates an interesting strategic question at the start of every match. Should I expand quickly to seize as many points as possible with these fragile, single-path networks? Or should I take it a bit slower and build in redundancies and more automated defenses? Both can work under certain circumstances.

The Necrons have some things in common with the AdMech playstyle, but they're also the most different of the four factions in terms of how their economy works. They are what I sometimes call a "goo faction," in that they want to spread their special kind of goo across the map. Think Zerg creep from Starcraft or Undead blight from Warcraft 3. Their specific goo is a green and black machine lattice that emanates from each Nexus of Dominion, fragile tower structures that also produce their only economic resource: dominion.

Basically, the Necron economy is based on how much of the map area you've managed to blanket in your power grid. This doesn't mean they don't care at all about resource points – capturing them can give powerful secondary benefits like reduced unit costs and increased production speed. But it does mean that they can keep expanding by going around heavily-defended points and gooping up uncontested corners of the map, which is a very interesting way to play.

The theme of the Necron army could be summed up by the declaration, "We are inevitable." Especially at the beginning of a match, they spread very slowly across the map. Swift scarabs are fast enough to seize some control points early, but don't have the staying power to hold them. Meanwhile, your core infantry unit, Necron Warriors, can even stand up to Space Marine Intercessors, but march incredibly slowly.

This makes certain map types that revolve around holding strategic points tricky for Necrons. They have some better fast units later, as well as limited access to teleportation. But against a swarmy faction like Orks, I usually had to resign myself to the fact that they would take an early lead in capture points, and I would simply have to wash over them like a slow-motion tide to wrap up the win decisively in the second half. Knowing when and where to commit is of the highest importance, because after deploying a wave of warriors or teleporting to a strategic location, the Necrons might not have a chance to pivot later.

They were only available in Skirmish, so I didn't get a great idea of what their campaign is about or who their face characters might be. But they're clearly getting set up as the big bads, so I'm interested to learn more about what their motives on Kronus will be.

While what I played is not a final build, I do have to mention some technical issues. There were a couple campaign missions that took upwards of two minutes to load, even on an SSD, and that's kind of unfortunate. Multiple times when a cutscene triggered in the middle of a mission, the entire client would hang for several seconds before proceeding. Hopefully these are all things that can be cleaned up before launch, which is barely over a month away on December 3.

Some technical scuff aside, I had a great time getting chromed up with the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Necrons in Dawn of War 4. The campaign story really starts to come together in some interesting ways in its second chapter. And the ways both of these factions control space differently feel like engaging and welcome additions to the roster compared to the more straightforward playstyle of Orks and Space Marines.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Leana Hafer is a contributing freelancer for IGN with a specialty in RPGs, strategy, horror, and survival games. She has been reviewing video games professionally since 2010 and is one of IGN's most prolific contributors, with more than 100 reviews published. You can also find her work on sites like PC Gamer and PCGamesN.

articles.title: Atlanta Dream sell out State Farm Arena for WNBA Finals Game 3
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream have officially sold out tickets for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena.
articles.body:
The Atlanta Dream have officially sold out tickets for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena.

The team confirmed the sellout to Channel 2 sports director Zach Klein. The Dream and Golden State Valkyries tip off Wednesday night at 8 p.m.

Channel 2 Action News broke the news last week that the Dream would be moving Game 3 and Game 4 from the Gateway Center to State Farm Arena.

The Dream worked closely with the Atlanta Hawks, State Farm Arena, WNBA and NBA to move schedules around to make it happen. The Dream also announced they would be moving to State Farm Arena for all their games starting in 2027.
